q: What are the Prometheus metric types: counter, gauge, histogram and summary?
p: Counters only increase, gauges go up and down, histograms bucket observations for aggregable quantiles, summaries compute quantiles client-side.
tip: Always use rate() on counters.
a: A counter is a cumulative value that only increases, or resets to zero on restart, such as requests served; its raw value is rarely useful, so I apply rate or increase, which handle resets. A gauge is a value that can go up and down, such as memory in use, queue length or temperature, and is read directly or with functions like avg_over_time. A histogram counts observations into configurable buckets and also keeps a sum and count; it allows calculating quantiles at query time with histogram_quantile and, importantly, aggregating across instances, so I prefer it for latency. A summary calculates quantiles on the client side, which is accurate for a single instance but cannot be aggregated across many. Bucket choice matters: they should surround the SLO thresholds. Newer native histograms improve resolution and cost. Choosing the right type determines whether the numbers are valid.
f: Why can histograms be aggregated but summaries not?
How do you pick bucket boundaries?

q: What is cardinality in metrics and how do you control it?
p: Cardinality is the number of unique label combinations; high-cardinality labels like user IDs explode memory and cost.
tip: Never label by unbounded values.
a: Each unique combination of metric name and label values creates a separate time series that the server must store and index. Labels with unbounded values, such as user IDs, email addresses, request URLs with identifiers or container IDs, can create millions of series, causing high memory use, slow queries and big bills in hosted systems. I control cardinality by designing labels from small, bounded sets such as method, route template and status class, never raw paths; dropping or aggregating unneeded labels with relabelling at scrape time; setting sample and series limits per target so one bad service cannot take down the monitoring; and using logs or traces for high-cardinality detail. I find offenders with queries that count series by metric and by label, and track series count as a metric with an alert. Churn from short-lived pods also contributes, so I watch both active and created series.
f: Which labels are dangerous?
How do you find high-cardinality metrics?

q: How do recording rules and federation help scale Prometheus?
p: Recording rules precompute expensive queries; federation or remote write aggregates data across servers.
cmds:
groups:
- name: slo
  rules:
  - record: job:http_requests:rate5m
    expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
tip: Dashboards should query recorded series.
a: Recording rules evaluate an expression at a regular interval and store the result as a new time series. Dashboards and alerts that use heavy expressions, such as quantiles over many series, then read the cheap precomputed series, making them fast and consistent. A naming convention like level:metric:operations keeps them understandable. For scale, a single Prometheus has limits on series count and retention, so I shard by team or environment and aggregate globally. Federation lets a central Prometheus scrape selected aggregated series from others, which works for summary views but is not meant to copy everything. For long-term storage and a global view, remote write to systems such as Thanos, Cortex, Mimir or a managed service is the common approach, with downsampling for older data. I keep high-resolution data local for alerting, since it must stay available when the network is not.
f: What is the naming convention for recorded series?
When use remote write instead of federation?

q: What is the USE method and how does it differ from RED?
p: USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) analyses resources; RED (rate, errors, duration) analyses request-driven services.
tip: USE for hosts, RED for services.
a: The USE method, from Brendan Gregg, examines every resource, such as CPU, memory, disks and network interfaces, for utilisation, meaning how busy it is, saturation, meaning queued or waiting work beyond capacity, and errors. It is a checklist for finding resource bottlenecks quickly. The RED method, from Tom Wilkie, suits microservices and focuses on rate of requests, number of errors and duration or latency. It describes the experience of the service's users. They complement each other: RED tells me a service is slow or failing, and USE helps find which underlying resource is the cause. The four golden signals from the SRE book, latency, traffic, errors and saturation, combine both ideas. In practice I build service dashboards with RED, infrastructure dashboards with USE, and link them so an engineer can move from symptom to cause.
f: Which method tells you the cause?
How do the golden signals relate?

q: How do you measure and alert on saturation, and why is it hard?
p: Saturation is how full a resource is; measure queue depth, throttling, run queue and utilisation against limits, and alert predictively.
tip: Queues reveal saturation before errors do.
a: Saturation means the system has more work than it can process immediately, so work queues up. It is hard because many resources saturate in non-obvious ways and utilisation alone misleads: a CPU at seventy percent average can still have throttled threads or a long run queue, and a thread pool can be exhausted while CPU is idle. Useful measures include run queue length and load relative to cores, CPU throttling in containers, memory pressure and swap activity, disk I/O queue depth and wait time, connection pool wait time, thread pool queue sizes, and message queue backlog. For capacity-like resources such as disk space, I use predictive alerts based on the trend, for example a linear forecast that the disk fills within four hours, which gives time to act. I treat sustained saturation as a leading indicator of latency and errors and often alert on it with lower urgency than user-facing symptoms.
f: Why is utilisation not enough?
What is a predictive alert?

q: How do you design log levels and what should be logged at each level?
p: Error for failures needing attention, warn for recoverable anomalies, info for key business events, debug for diagnostics; avoid noise and secrets.
tip: Every error log should be actionable.
a: Levels communicate importance and control volume. Error means an operation failed in a way that someone may need to act on, and should include context and the exception. Warning marks unexpected but handled situations, such as a retry or fallback, that might indicate a developing problem. Info records significant lifecycle and business events, like service start, configuration loaded or an order placed, at a rate that is affordable in production. Debug and trace are detailed diagnostics, normally disabled in production, or enabled temporarily per component or request. I avoid logging inside tight loops, avoid logging the same error at every layer as it propagates, and never log secrets, tokens or personal data. Logs should be structured with consistent field names, a correlation or trace identifier and enough context to reproduce the issue. Reviewing logs periodically for noise keeps the signal useful and costs under control.
f: What should every error log contain?
Why not log the same exception at each layer?

q: How do you handle sensitive data and compliance in logs?
p: Do not log secrets or personal data; mask or hash at source, restrict access, set retention and audit log access.
tip: Redact at the source, not later.
a: Logs are often copied to many systems and retained for long, so sensitive data in them becomes a liability under privacy and security rules. The first line of defence is not logging it: developers avoid printing request bodies, headers with tokens, passwords, card numbers and personal identifiers, with libraries or lint rules that help. Where fields are needed, I mask, truncate or hash them at the source, and add redaction rules in the collection pipeline as a safety net, using pattern matching for known formats. Access to logs is restricted by role, with audit trails of who searched what, and sensitive streams such as authentication or payment logs get stricter controls and shorter retention. Retention periods match legal requirements and operational need, and deletion requests must be feasible, which another reason for keeping personal data out. Encrypt in transit and at rest, and test the pipeline for leaks periodically.
f: Why redact at the source?
How do retention rules help compliance?

q: What is log sampling and when is it appropriate?
p: Keep a representative fraction of high-volume low-value logs while always keeping errors and rare events.
tip: Sample by request ID to keep complete flows.
a: At high traffic, logging every successful request at info level can be enormously expensive and mostly redundant. Sampling reduces volume by keeping a fraction, perhaps five percent of routine events, while always retaining errors, warnings and slow requests. To keep logs useful, I sample consistently by request or trace identifier so that either all log lines of a request are kept or none, which preserves the story; random per-line sampling produces fragments. Rate-limited logging prevents a failing loop from emitting millions of identical lines, with a counter of suppressed messages. Metrics should cover what sampled logs omit, since counts and rates need to be exact; I never derive metrics from sampled logs. Dynamic sampling can raise the rate temporarily during incidents. Tail-based approaches in a collector decide after seeing the whole request, keeping interesting ones. Sampling should be documented so responders know what might be missing.
f: Why sample by request ID?
Why not compute metrics from sampled logs?

q: How do you query logs effectively in Loki with LogQL or in Elasticsearch?
p: Filter by indexed labels first, then line filters and parsers; avoid broad regexes over long ranges.
tip: Labels select streams; filters scan text.
a: In Loki, only labels are indexed, so a query starts with a stream selector using labels like app, namespace and environment to narrow to the relevant streams, then applies line filters such as contains or regex, then parsers like json or logfmt to extract fields, and finally filters or aggregates on extracted fields. The earlier I narrow, the less data is scanned, so I avoid selectors that match everything and keep the time range tight. LogQL can also compute metrics from logs, like error rates by route, useful for ad hoc analysis or alerts. In Elasticsearch, the whole text is indexed, so queries use the query DSL or KQL on fields, with time filters first; keyword fields are exact, while text fields are analysed. For both systems I make sure logs are structured with consistent fields, which makes queries simple, and create saved queries and dashboards for common investigations.
f: Why are labels special in Loki?
When convert logs to metrics?

q: What are the trade-offs between agent-based, sidecar and direct logging pipelines?
p: Node agents are efficient and simple; sidecars isolate per-app needs; direct SDK shipping couples the app to the backend and risks loss.
tip: Buffer on disk to survive outages.
a: A node-level agent, running as a daemonset, tails container log files on each node and ships them, which uses few resources and needs no changes to applications, making it the default. A sidecar per pod suits cases where an application writes to files, needs special parsing or has to send to a different destination, but adds resource overhead for every pod and operational complexity. Direct shipping from the application via a logging SDK avoids files but couples the app to the backend, adds latency and can lose logs or block the application if the backend is down. Whatever the approach, I design for backpressure and failure: use disk buffering in agents, bounded queues, retries with backoff, and drop policies that protect the application. A central aggregation layer, such as a collector or message queue, absorbs bursts, allows routing and filtering, and decouples producers from storage. I monitor the pipeline's own health, including dropped and delayed logs.
f: When is a sidecar justified?
How do you protect apps from logging backpressure?

q: What is trace sampling and how do head-based and tail-based sampling differ?
p: Head sampling decides at the start of a trace; tail sampling decides after seeing the whole trace, so it can keep errors and slow traces.
cmds:
processors:
  tail_sampling:
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]}
tip: Tail sampling needs all spans of a trace in one place.
a: Storing every trace at high traffic is too expensive, so we sample. Head-based sampling makes a decision when the trace begins, such as keep ten percent, and propagates the decision to all services. It is simple and cheap but blind: it may discard the rare slow or failed request I most want. Tail-based sampling waits until the trace is complete, usually in a collector, and then applies policies, such as keep all traces with errors, keep those slower than a threshold, and a small random fraction of the rest. It captures the interesting traces but requires buffering all spans of a trace in memory and routing all spans for a trace to the same collector instance, which adds complexity and cost. Many systems combine them: a modest head sample plus tail rules. Metrics derived from spans before sampling keep rates accurate.
f: Why is head sampling blind?
What does tail sampling require?

q: What is context propagation and what breaks it?
p: Trace identifiers travel in headers or message metadata so spans link across services; breaks occur at async boundaries, proxies and unsupported libraries.
tip: Instrument queues and thread pools explicitly.
a: For a trace to span multiple services, each service must receive the trace context from the caller and pass it on to callees. The W3C Trace Context standard defines the traceparent header with the trace identifier, parent span identifier and flags, and baggage can carry extra key-value data. Instrumentation libraries inject and extract these automatically for common HTTP and gRPC clients and servers. Propagation breaks at boundaries the library does not cover: message queues, where context must be placed in message headers; background jobs and thread pools, where the context does not automatically move to another thread; proxies, gateways or load balancers that strip unknown headers; and services using different propagation formats, such as older B3 headers. Symptoms are broken traces, orphan spans and traces that begin in the middle. I fix these by configuring consistent propagators, instrumenting messaging and async hand-offs, and checking gateways, then verifying with a test request through the full path.
f: Which header carries trace context?
Why do queues break traces?

q: How do you use span attributes, events and links wisely?
p: Attributes describe a span with bounded, queryable data; events mark moments inside it; links connect causally related traces such as batch consumers.
tip: Use semantic convention names.
a: Attributes are key-value metadata that make spans searchable and filterable, such as route template, status code, database system, tenant or feature flag. I follow OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for names so tools understand them, use bounded values for anything I plan to group by, and avoid putting secrets or huge payloads in them. Events are timestamped annotations within a span, for example a retry, cache miss or exception, that explain what happened during its lifetime without creating a full child span. Links connect spans that are related but not parent and child, such as a batch consumer processing many messages, each from a different producer trace, or a retry that references the original attempt. Good instrumentation creates spans for meaningful operations, like outgoing calls and significant internal steps, but not for every function, which adds overhead and noise. Consistent attributes make traces answer questions quickly.
f: What are semantic conventions?
When use a link instead of a parent?

q: How do you read a trace waterfall to find a latency problem?
p: Look for the longest spans, gaps with no child work, serial calls that could be parallel, repeated calls and retries.
tip: Gaps often mean waiting, not working.
a: In the waterfall each span is a bar positioned in time, with children nested under parents. I first find the critical path: the chain of spans that determines the total duration. A long span with little child activity may be the actual work in that service, or it may be waiting. Gaps between a parent's start and its first child, or between children, point to queueing, lock waits, thread pool starvation or garbage collection pauses. A staircase of sequential calls that do not depend on each other suggests an opportunity for parallelism. Many small repeated spans to the same database indicate an N plus one query pattern. Spans with retries or timeouts show dependency instability. Comparing a slow trace with a fast one for the same route highlights the differing step. Then I use the span attributes and linked logs to confirm the cause before changing anything.
f: What does a gap in the waterfall indicate?
How do you spot an N+1 pattern?

q: How do you derive RED metrics from traces, and what are span metrics?
p: A collector connector aggregates spans into request count, error count and duration histograms, giving metrics without extra instrumentation.
tip: Generate before sampling to keep counts exact.
a: Span metrics convert tracing data into metrics: the OpenTelemetry collector's spanmetrics connector, or backend features in Tempo and others, count spans and measure durations per service, operation and status, producing request rate, error rate and latency histograms. This gives RED metrics for every instrumented service with no separate metric instrumentation, and ties metrics to the same naming as traces. The critical point is to generate them before sampling, otherwise counts would reflect the sample rather than real traffic. I keep dimensions bounded, using service, route template and status code, never raw identifiers, to avoid cardinality blowups. These metrics can power dashboards and SLO alerts, and exemplars on the histograms link a latency spike to representative traces. It is a good way to get consistent baseline monitoring across heterogeneous services, though application-specific business metrics still need explicit instrumentation.
f: Why generate metrics before sampling?
What dimensions should be used?

q: What is multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting?
p: Alert when the error budget burns quickly over both a long and short window, catching fast and slow burns while avoiding flapping.
tip: Short window confirms it is still happening.
a: Burn rate is how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the rate that would exactly exhaust it at the end of the SLO window. A burn rate of one uses the budget in precisely the full period; fourteen point four over one hour consumes two percent of a thirty-day budget. A multi-window approach pairs a long window, which provides significance, with a short window, which shows the problem is ongoing and lets the alert reset quickly after recovery. Typically I use several tiers: a high burn rate over one hour and five minutes pages immediately for severe outages; a moderate burn over six hours and thirty minutes pages for slower serious problems; and a low burn over days creates a ticket. This design catches both sudden outages and slow degradations with few false alarms, and ties urgency directly to the user-facing objective and the remaining budget.
f: What does a burn rate of 1 mean?
Why combine two windows?

q: How do you write alert annotations and runbook links that help on-call responders?
p: Include summary, impact, severity, the dashboard and runbook URL, and likely first checks so the responder can act in minutes.
cmds:
annotations:
  summary: 'Checkout error rate above SLO burn threshold'
  runbook_url: https://runbooks.example/checkout-errors
  dashboard: https://grafana.example/d/checkout
tip: The alert should answer: what, how bad, what now.
a: An alert is a message to a tired human, so it must carry enough context to act. The title states what is wrong in plain language, not an internal metric name. The description gives the scope and impact, for example which service, which region, the current value and threshold, and how long it has lasted. Labels set severity and the owning team for routing. Links go to the relevant dashboard filtered to the right time and service, to the runbook with diagnostic steps and known remediations, and perhaps to recent deployments. A runbook should start with quick checks and decision points, include commands, escalation contacts and rollback steps, and be tested and updated after incidents. I review alerts regularly: any alert that did not require action should be fixed or removed, and any incident without a good alert reveals a gap. Templates enforce the standard.
f: What should every alert include?
How do you keep runbooks current?

q: How do you reduce alert noise with grouping, inhibition and deduplication?
p: Group related alerts into one notification, inhibit symptom alerts when a root-cause alert fires, and deduplicate repeated firings.
cmds:
route:
  group_by: [alertname, cluster]
  group_wait: 30s
inhibit_rules:
- source_matchers: [alertname="NodeDown"]
  target_matchers: [alertname="PodNotReady"]
  equal: [node]
tip: One incident should be one page.
a: During a failure, dozens of alerts may fire from one root cause: a node down triggers pod, service and latency alerts. Alertmanager helps by grouping alerts by labels like cluster and alert name into a single notification, with a short group wait to collect related ones. Inhibition rules suppress lower-level alerts when a higher-level one is firing, such as hiding pod readiness alerts for a node already reported down. Deduplication ensures that repeated evaluations of the same alert do not create new pages, and repeat intervals control reminders. Routing sends alerts to the right team and channel by severity, and time-based muting suppresses expected noise during maintenance windows through silences. Beyond tooling, the best noise reduction is better alert design: alert on symptoms rather than causes, set sensible durations, and delete alerts nobody acts on. I track pages per shift as a health metric for the on-call rotation.
f: What does inhibition do?
Why group by cluster?

q: What is the difference between alerting on symptoms versus causes, and which should page?
p: Symptoms are user-visible failures and should page; causes are internal conditions best used for diagnosis or tickets.
cmds:
# page: error rate and latency SLO burn
# ticket: disk 80% full, node memory high
tip: Page on what users feel.
a: A symptom alert reports that users are being harmed or soon will be, such as elevated error rate, high latency or failed checkouts. A cause alert reports an internal condition like high CPU, a restart, a full queue or a lagging replica, which may or may not lead to user impact. Paging on causes generates many false alarms because systems often tolerate high CPU or restarts without harm, and it also misses failures whose cause I did not anticipate. Paging on symptoms catches any cause. Cause-oriented alerts still have a place as warnings or tickets, for predictable resource exhaustion that needs action before it becomes user-visible, such as disk filling in a day, and as diagnostic panels on dashboards. The resulting structure is a small number of high-signal pages tied to service objectives, supported by richer diagnostic data to find the cause quickly.
f: Why do cause alerts cause false pages?
Where do predictive disk alerts belong?

q: How do you test alerts and make sure they actually fire?
p: Unit-test rules with promtool, inject synthetic failures, use a dead man's switch, and run game days to validate the full path.
tip: An alert never tested is a hope.
a: Alerting rules are code and need tests. With promtool I write unit tests that feed synthetic time series into rules and assert which alerts fire at specific times, which catches typos and logic mistakes in expressions and for durations. To validate the whole chain, I use a watchdog alert that always fires and is routed to an external dead man's switch service, which notifies me if it stops arriving, meaning Prometheus, Alertmanager or the network path to the pager is broken. I also run controlled experiments, such as injecting errors or latency in staging, or in production game days, and confirm that the right alert fires, reaches the right person and has a useful runbook. After each incident I check whether the alerts fired as expected and how long detection took, and fix gaps. Regularly auditing rules for missing metrics prevents silent failures.
f: What does a dead man's switch detect?
How does promtool test rules?

q: How do you choose good SLIs for different types of services?
p: Pick indicators users feel: availability and latency for request services, freshness and correctness for pipelines, durability for storage.
tip: Measure close to the user.
a: A service-level indicator is a measurable proportion of good events over valid events. For request-driven services the common SLIs are availability, the fraction of requests that succeed, and latency, the fraction faster than a threshold, measured at the load balancer or client edge so they reflect the user's experience. For batch and data pipelines, freshness, meaning how recently the data was updated, correctness and throughput are better. For storage systems, durability and availability of reads and writes matter. Critical user journeys, like login or checkout, deserve their own SLIs, and I validate the indicator against real incidents: if users were unhappy while the SLI was green, it is wrong. Thresholds should come from user expectations and what is achievable, not arbitrary. I keep the number of SLIs per service small, exclude invalid events such as bad client requests, and define them in a shared template.
f: What is a good-over-valid ratio?
How do you validate an SLI?

q: How do you set an SLO target and negotiate it with product owners?
p: Base it on user needs and historical performance, make it slightly below what users would notice, and agree what happens when the budget is spent.
cmds: # 99.9% over 30 days = 43.2 minutes of error budget
tip: 100% is the wrong target.
a: I start with data: what has the service actually achieved over the last months, and what do users need? A target should be tight enough that violations mean unhappy users but loose enough to be achievable and leave room for change, since each additional nine costs exponentially more and slows feature delivery. With product owners I convert targets into concrete terms: 99.9 percent over thirty days allows about 43 minutes of downtime, and ask whether that meets expectations. The negotiation also covers the error budget policy: what happens when the budget is nearly spent, for example pausing risky launches and focusing on reliability work, and what happens when there is plenty left, such as faster releases and experiments. I document it, review it quarterly, and adjust as the product matures. Internal SLOs should be stricter than any external SLA to give a buffer.
f: Why is 100% a bad target?
What is an error budget policy?

q: How do you handle SLOs for dependencies and composite services?
p: Availability multiplies across serial dependencies; set dependency SLOs higher than yours and use redundancy, fallbacks and caching to decouple.
tip: Serial dependencies erode availability.
a: If a request needs three services in series, each at 99.9 percent, the combined availability is roughly 99.7 percent, so a service cannot promise more than its critical dependencies provide. This arithmetic drives design. I identify which dependencies are hard, whose failure fails the request, and which are soft and can degrade gracefully. For hard dependencies I require SLOs higher than my own target and track their actual performance, and I reduce coupling with caching, fallbacks, timeouts, retries with budgets, circuit breakers and asynchronous processing. Redundancy across zones or providers improves effective availability for dependencies I control. When I report my SLI, I measure from the user's perspective so dependency failures count, but I also attribute budget burn to causes, which tells where investment pays off. Agreements with other teams, such as internal SLAs, make expectations explicit and provide a basis for prioritising reliability work.
f: How does serial availability compound?
What is a soft dependency?

q: How do you report SLO status to leadership and use it in planning?
p: Show compliance, remaining budget and burn trends in simple dashboards and reviews, link breaches to actions, and use it to prioritise reliability work.
tip: Make the budget visible weekly.
a: Leaders need a clear, regular view, not a wall of graphs. For each critical service I show the SLO target, the current compliance over the window, the percentage of error budget remaining and the recent burn trend, with a status indicator. A monthly or quarterly reliability review looks at services that missed or are close to missing their objectives, the incidents that consumed budget, and the actions taken. This connects reliability to planning: services with exhausted budgets get reliability work prioritised, in line with the agreed policy, while services with healthy budgets can ship faster. I highlight the largest causes of budget loss, such as a recurring dependency failure, so investments target the biggest wins, and I translate technical numbers into user and business impact where possible. Consistent definitions across teams allow comparison, and honest reporting, including misses, builds credibility for the process.
f: What belongs on an SLO status page?
How does budget status affect planning?

q: What is the difference between SLA, SLO and SLI in practice, and what happens when an SLA is breached?
p: SLI is the measurement, SLO the internal target, SLA a contract with consequences like credits; keep the SLO stricter than the SLA.
cmds: # SLI: 99.95% good requests; SLO: 99.9%; SLA: 99.5% with credits
tip: SLA breaches cost money, SLO breaches cost focus.
a: An SLI is a measured value, such as the proportion of requests served successfully. An SLO is the target the team sets for that SLI over a period, and it drives internal decisions through the error budget. An SLA is a contractual commitment to customers, usually less strict than the internal SLO, with defined remedies such as service credits or termination rights if it is not met. In practice, I keep the SLO stricter than the SLA so that internal alarms and corrective action occur before contractual breach. When an SLO is missed, the consequence is internal: reliability work takes priority and releases may slow. When an SLA is breached, there are financial and reputational consequences, a formal notification and calculation of credits, and a thorough postmortem for customers. The SLA's definitions of what counts as downtime, measurement windows and exclusions need careful legal and engineering review.
f: Why is the SLO stricter than the SLA?
What is the consequence of each breach?

q: How do you structure dashboards: overview, service and deep-dive levels?
p: Layered dashboards move from health overview to service RED panels to detailed resources, with consistent layout and drill-down links.
cmds: # row 1: SLO status; row 2: RED; row 3: dependencies; row 4: resources
tip: Same layout for every service.
a: During an incident people need to go from what is wrong to why in minutes. I create a top-level overview showing the health of all key services and SLO status, with colour coding and links. Each service has a standard dashboard with the same layout: SLO and error budget at the top, then request rate, errors and latency, then dependency health, then resource saturation such as CPU, memory and connection pools, and finally recent deployments or annotations. Deep-dive dashboards cover specific technologies like Kubernetes nodes, databases or caches. Consistency matters, because responders can read any service's dashboard without learning a new layout, and generating dashboards from code or templates ensures it. Variables for cluster, namespace and service avoid duplicates, and links carry the time range and filters between levels. I remove panels that no one uses and review dashboards after incidents.
f: What goes at the top of a service dashboard?
Why generate dashboards from code?

q: What are Grafana annotations and how do they help correlate changes with incidents?
p: Annotations mark events such as deploys, config changes and incidents on graphs, showing what changed when behaviour shifted.
tip: Most incidents follow a change.
a: A large share of incidents are caused by changes, so seeing change events on the same timeline as metrics greatly speeds diagnosis. Grafana annotations overlay vertical markers on panels for events, which can be added through the API from the CI/CD pipeline at each deployment, from configuration management, feature flag changes, scaling events or manual incident markers. They can also be queried from a data source, such as a metric or log query that identifies restarts or alerts. I include tags for service, environment and version so dashboards can filter annotations relevant to them. During an investigation, a latency jump that lines up exactly with a deploy marker immediately suggests a rollback, while no nearby change suggests looking at traffic or dependencies. Annotations also help postmortems build timelines accurately. Making the pipeline emit them is a small investment with a large payoff.
f: What events should be annotated?
How are annotations created automatically?

q: How do you avoid misleading visualisations such as averages, misaligned axes and missing data?
p: Use percentiles or heatmaps for latency, label units, start axes sensibly, handle gaps explicitly, and show sample sizes.
tip: Averages hide tail latency.
a: Averages hide the experience of the slowest users; latency should be shown with percentiles such as p50, p95 and p99, or as heatmaps of the distribution. Mean error rates over long windows can hide short severe outages, so I choose resolution suited to the question. Other pitfalls include inconsistent or missing units, truncated axes that exaggerate small changes or zero-based axes that hide important ones, stacked graphs that make individual series hard to read, and too many lines. Missing data should be visible: a gap because a target stopped reporting is different from zero, and a dashboard that shows zero errors because the metric disappeared is dangerously misleading, so I add panels for data presence and alert on absent metrics. Rates computed over very small sample sizes are noisy, so I show request counts alongside. Clear titles, descriptions, thresholds and consistent colours make a dashboard trustworthy.
f: Why are averages misleading for latency?
How do you detect missing data?

q: How do you build dashboards-as-code and manage them with GitOps?
p: Define dashboards with Jsonnet, Grafonnet, Terraform or provisioning files in Git, review changes, and deploy automatically.
tip: Stop editing production dashboards by hand.
a: Dashboards edited by hand in the UI drift, break silently and cannot be reviewed or reproduced. Treating them as code solves this. I define them with a library like Grafonnet or Jsonnet, the Grafana Terraform provider, or provisioned JSON files, and keep them in Git. Templates generate the standard service dashboard for each service from a list, so consistency is enforced and a change to the template updates all of them. Pull requests provide review, and CI validates the output, for example by linting the JSON or checking queries. A pipeline or the Grafana operator then deploys them to environments. UI editing is still allowed for experimentation, but changes that matter are exported back to code, and production provisioning can be set read-only to prevent drift. This approach gives history, rollback, reuse across environments and disaster recovery.
f: Why use templates for service dashboards?
How do you prevent drift?

q: How would you build a dashboard for a business-critical user journey, such as checkout?
p: Combine funnel conversion, step latency and errors, dependency health and synthetic checks so engineering and business see the same story.
tip: Include a business metric next to technical ones.
a: I begin from the journey: cart, address, payment, confirmation. For each step I show success rate and latency, and a funnel of conversion between steps, which reveals drop-offs that technical metrics alone might miss. Next to it, I show the technical dependencies supporting the journey: payment provider latency and errors, inventory service, database and cache health, along with SLO burn for the journey. Synthetic probes that perform a test purchase continuously give an outside-in measure and detect problems even at low traffic. Deploy and feature flag annotations help correlation. A business metric, such as orders per minute compared to the same time last week, shows impact in terms everyone understands. Alerts for the journey are linked from the dashboard. A shared dashboard used by engineering, support and product creates a common picture during incidents and reduces back-and-forth.
f: Why include a synthetic probe?
Why add a week-over-week comparison?

q: How do Thanos, Cortex and Mimir extend Prometheus for long-term storage and global views?
p: They accept remote-written or sidecar-uploaded data, store it in object storage, and provide global query, downsampling and multi-tenancy.
tip: Keep local Prometheus for alerting.
a: A single Prometheus keeps data locally for a limited time and is not horizontally scalable. Thanos adds a sidecar that uploads blocks to object storage, a store gateway to read them, a querier that merges data from many Prometheus instances and storage into one global view, and a compactor that downsamples for cheaper long-range queries. Cortex and Mimir take a different approach: Prometheus servers remote write to a horizontally scalable, multi-tenant backend with distributors, ingesters and queriers, storing blocks in object storage, which suits large central platforms and SaaS-like setups. Both give long retention, high availability through replication or deduplication, and global queries across clusters. I keep local Prometheus instances for scraping and alerting so alerts do not depend on the central system, and use the long-term system for dashboards, history and capacity planning. Cost control comes from cardinality management and downsampling.
f: What does the Thanos compactor do?
Why keep alerting local?

q: What is the OpenTelemetry Collector and why use it?
p: A vendor-neutral pipeline of receivers, processors and exporters that ingests, enriches, samples and routes telemetry.
tip: Run agents per node and a gateway tier.
a: The Collector is a standalone service that receives telemetry in many formats, processes it, and exports to one or more backends. Receivers accept OTLP, Prometheus scrapes, Jaeger, Zipkin and logs. Processors batch data for efficiency, limit memory, add Kubernetes metadata such as pod and namespace, redact sensitive attributes, filter noise and perform tail sampling. Exporters send data to the chosen backends, and can fan out to multiple destinations. Using a collector decouples applications from vendors: apps send OTLP to a local endpoint, and changing backends becomes a configuration change. A typical deployment runs a daemonset agent on each node for local collection and enrichment, and a gateway deployment for heavier processing such as tail sampling and routing. Production considerations are sizing, memory limiters, queues and retries for backpressure, health monitoring of the collector itself, and managing configuration through version control.
f: What are receivers, processors and exporters?
Why use agent and gateway tiers?

q: How do you choose between self-hosted open-source observability and a commercial SaaS platform?
p: Weigh cost at scale, operational effort, features, data control, lock-in and team skills; many use a hybrid with OpenTelemetry for portability.
cmds: # criteria: cost model, retention, cardinality limits, compliance, support, exit plan
tip: Instrument with open standards either way.
a: Self-hosted tools like Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and Grafana offer control, flexibility, no per-host licensing and data kept in my environment, but need engineers to run, scale, secure and upgrade them, and incident tooling can be fragmented. Commercial platforms provide integrated metrics, logs, traces, alerting and analysis out of the box, fast onboarding, support and advanced features, but pricing based on hosts, ingestion or custom metrics can grow steeply and surprise teams, and there is a risk of lock-in. My decision criteria include total cost at expected scale including engineer time, compliance and data residency requirements, retention and cardinality needs, team capacity and skills, and desired features. A pragmatic path is to instrument with OpenTelemetry and open metric formats so backends can change, and potentially mix: for example managed Prometheus for metrics and a SaaS for traces. Budgets and cost governance are needed in either case.
f: Why instrument with OpenTelemetry?
What drives SaaS cost?

q: What is eBPF-based observability and what are its benefits and limits?
p: eBPF programs run in the kernel to collect network, process and security telemetry with low overhead and no code changes.
tip: Needs kernel support and privileges.
a: eBPF lets small, verified programs run safely inside the Linux kernel, attached to events like system calls, network packets and function entry points. Observability tools use it to collect telemetry without modifying or restarting applications: network flows and DNS visibility between services, latency of TCP connections, CPU profiles, file and process activity, and even automatic HTTP or database request tracing by parsing traffic. Examples include Cilium's Hubble, Pixie, Parca and Falco for security. Benefits are low overhead, broad coverage including legacy or third-party software, and visibility from the kernel's perspective that application instrumentation can miss. Limits include the need for fairly recent kernels and elevated privileges, difficulty decoding encrypted traffic without hooks into libraries, less business-level context than application traces, operational risk if poorly configured, and cost of the data volume. I treat it as a complement to OpenTelemetry instrumentation, not a replacement.
f: What does eBPF let you observe?
What are its limits?

q: How do synthetic monitoring and real user monitoring differ and when do you need each?
p: Synthetic checks run scripted probes continuously from outside; RUM measures actual user sessions in browsers. Together they show availability and real experience.
cmds: blackbox_exporter probe module: http_2xx target: https://shop.example
tip: Synthetics find outages at 3 a.m. with no traffic.
a: Synthetic monitoring runs scripted requests or browser journeys from chosen locations at regular intervals. It gives consistent baselines, detects outages even when there is no user traffic, tests critical flows end to end such as login and checkout, and measures from outside the infrastructure, so it also catches DNS, CDN or certificate issues. Its limitation is that it covers only the scenarios I script, from a few locations. Real user monitoring instruments the actual browser or mobile app, collecting page load timings, web vitals, JavaScript errors and network failures from real devices, networks and regions, showing what users truly experience, including problems specific to a browser version or country. It depends on traffic and has privacy considerations. I use synthetic checks for availability alerts and SLOs on key journeys, and RUM for performance analysis and prioritisation. Correlating both with backend traces gives the full picture.
f: What can synthetic monitoring catch that RUM cannot?
What privacy issues does RUM have?

q: How do you monitor Kubernetes control-plane health: API server, etcd and scheduler?
p: Track API request latency and errors, etcd disk sync and leader changes, scheduler queue and pending pods, and controller work queues.
tip: etcd is sensitive to disk latency.
a: On self-managed clusters the control plane is critical, and even on managed ones some metrics are exposed. For the API server I watch request rate, error rate and latency by verb and resource, inflight requests and priority and fairness rejections. For etcd, key signals are write-ahead log fsync and backend commit durations, which reflect disk speed, leader changes, proposals failed or pending, database size against quota and the number of members up. The scheduler's pending pod count and scheduling latency show capacity or constraint issues; the controller manager's work queue depth and retries show reconciliation problems. Certificate expiry for control-plane components is another classic outage cause. I alert when the API server error rate or latency is high, etcd has no leader or frequent leader elections, or database size nears the quota. Slow admission webhooks are a hidden cause of API latency, so I monitor them too.
f: Why is etcd disk latency crucial?
What can slow the API server besides load?

q: How do you use kube-state-metrics and cAdvisor, and what is the difference?
p: kube-state-metrics reports object state from the API; cAdvisor reports container resource usage from the kubelet.
tip: State vs usage.
a: They answer different questions. Kube-state-metrics listens to the Kubernetes API and generates metrics about the desired and current state of objects: deployments' available replicas, pod phase, container waiting reasons like CrashLoopBackOff, job success, node conditions, resource requests and limits, persistent volume claim status. cAdvisor, built into the kubelet, measures actual resource consumption of each container: CPU time, memory working set, network and disk I/O, and CPU throttling. Combining the two is powerful: comparing usage with requests and limits shows over- and under-provisioning, and state metrics tell me why a pod is not running while usage metrics tell me how it behaves when running. Typical alerts use state metrics such as unavailable replicas or pods stuck pending, while capacity planning and right-sizing use usage metrics. Both are deployed by kube-prometheus-stack and need label joins to attach owner information such as the deployment name.
f: Which tool shows CrashLoopBackOff?
How do you right-size from these metrics?

q: How do you find noisy neighbours and right-size workloads using metrics?
p: Compare usage against requests per workload over weeks, look at percentiles and throttling, and use VPA recommendations.
tip: Use p95 over a long window.
a: I compute, for each workload, the ratio of actual usage to the requested amount using percentiles over a long enough period to include peaks, such as the ninety-fifth percentile over two weeks. Workloads using far less than requested waste money and block scheduling; those near or above limits risk throttling or OOM kills. I include CPU throttling metrics and restart reasons to catch workloads constrained in ways usage hides. For noisy neighbours, I look at nodes with high CPU steal, memory pressure or disk and network saturation and identify the top consumers by node. The vertical pod autoscaler in recommendation mode analyses history and suggests requests, which I apply gradually and review rather than blindly automating. Namespace quotas and limit ranges keep teams within bounds, and cost tools allocate spend to owners. Right-sizing is a continuous process, repeated after significant changes in load or code.
f: Why use p95 over a long window?
What does VPA recommendation mode do?

q: How do you monitor pod restarts, OOM kills and evictions meaningfully?
p: Alert on restart rate and last termination reason, not raw counts; separate OOMKilled from errors and evictions from node pressure.
tip: Reason labels tell you the fix.
a: A restart counter by itself is noisy; what matters is the rate and the reason. I alert when a container restarts several times within an hour, using increase over a window, and enrich the alert with the last termination reason from kube-state-metrics. OOMKilled points to memory limits or leaks and leads to checking memory trends and heap settings. A non-zero exit code with error reason suggests an application crash, so I look at previous logs. Evictions happen when the node is under pressure, such as memory or disk, and I correlate them with node metrics and with pods' QoS classes; many evictions on a node suggest requests are too low or the node is overcommitted. CrashLoopBackOff waiting reasons are alerted separately. Dashboards show restarts by workload to spot patterns after deploys. Each alert links to a runbook with the relevant kubectl describe, logs and metrics steps.
f: How do you tell OOM from an application crash?
What causes evictions?

q: How do you set up multi-cluster monitoring and consistent labelling?
p: Add cluster, region and environment external labels, ship to a central store, and use consistent label schemas for dashboards and alerts.
cmds:
global:
  external_labels:
    cluster: prod-eu-1
    region: eu-west-1
tip: Add the cluster label at the source.
a: With many clusters, I give each Prometheus or agent external labels such as cluster, region and environment, so every series and alert carries its origin. Metrics are shipped to a central store using remote write, or queried globally with Thanos, and logs and traces are tagged with the same attributes through the collectors. Dashboards use a cluster variable, so one dashboard serves all clusters, and alert rules are written once and deployed everywhere, with the cluster label used in routing and annotations. A consistent label schema across telemetry is essential: the same names for service, namespace, team and version, following OpenTelemetry resource conventions, so I can pivot between metrics, logs and traces. Ownership labels enable routing alerts to the right team. I also monitor the monitoring: each cluster's agent health, scrape failures and remote write lag, with a watchdog alert so silent failures are noticed.
f: Why use external labels?
How do you monitor the monitoring system?

q: How do you monitor serverless functions such as Lambda or Cloud Functions?
p: Track invocations, errors, duration, throttles and cold starts, use structured logs and distributed tracing, and alert on error rate and concurrency limits.
tip: Cold starts show up in tail latency.
a: Serverless removes servers to manage but not the need for observability. The platform provides core metrics: invocation count, errors, duration percentiles, throttles when concurrency limits are hit, and iterator age for stream triggers. I alert on error rate, throttling, and duration approaching the timeout. Cold starts add latency to a fraction of invocations, visible in tail latency and in init duration metrics, and mitigated with provisioned concurrency, smaller packages or lighter runtimes. Logs are written to the platform's logging service; I use structured JSON with request identifiers and keep log volume reasonable, as it affects cost. Distributed tracing, through OpenTelemetry layers or the provider's tracing integration, links functions with the services they call and with queues or API gateways. I also monitor downstream limits like database connections that functions can exhaust when scaling quickly, and track cost per invocation as a signal.
f: What causes throttles in Lambda?
How do cold starts show up in metrics?

q: How do you control observability costs in the cloud?
p: Manage cardinality, sampling, retention tiers, log volume and duplicate collection, with budgets, ownership and dashboards of telemetry spend.
tip: Observability is often the second-largest bill.
a: Telemetry costs grow quickly with scale. I attack it from several angles. For metrics, limit label cardinality, drop unused metrics at scrape time and set longer scrape intervals for low-value targets. For logs, reduce verbosity, sample routine events, drop health-check noise, filter before ingestion, and use cheaper storage tiers or archives for older logs with short searchable retention. For traces, apply tail sampling to keep errors and slow requests and a small fraction of the rest. I remove duplicates, such as the same logs collected twice, and unused dashboards and queries. Visibility drives behaviour: I track ingestion volume and cost by team and service, set budgets and alerts, and make owners accountable. Retention should reflect need: seven days of detailed data is often enough for debugging, with aggregates kept for longer. Costs must be balanced against the risk of losing data needed during an incident.
f: Where do telemetry costs come from?
How do you make teams accountable for them?

q: How do you build a cross-account or cross-project logging and monitoring architecture?
p: Centralise into a dedicated observability account or project with delegated, read-only access, aggregation sinks and strict IAM and encryption.
cmds: gcloud logging sinks create central-sink storage.googleapis.com/bucket --include-children --organization=ORG
tip: Write-only from workloads, read-controlled centrally.
a: In multi-account organisations, each workload account would otherwise keep its own islands of logs and metrics. A common design is a dedicated observability or logging account or project. Workload accounts send logs and metrics through sinks, subscription filters or agents to central storage, with write-only permissions so a compromised workload cannot alter or delete the central copy. Organisation-level sinks automatically capture audit logs from new accounts. The central platform provides search, dashboards, alerting and long retention, with role-based access so teams see their own data and security teams see audit streams. Data is encrypted with managed keys, transfer costs are considered, and residency rules may require regional aggregation. Metrics may stay local for alerting while summaries flow centrally. Infrastructure as code deploys the agents, sinks and permissions consistently so that a new account is observable from day one.
f: Why write-only access from workloads?
What is an organisation-level sink?

q: How do you use cloud-native tracing and profiling such as X-Ray, Cloud Trace and Cloud Profiler?
p: Instrument or enable integrations to trace requests across managed services, and use continuous profilers to find CPU and memory hotspots in production.
tip: Continuous profiling has very low overhead.
a: Cloud providers offer tracing services that integrate with their managed products such as load balancers, functions, queues and databases, giving traces that include those services without much manual work, plus application SDKs or OpenTelemetry exporters for custom code. Traces show the path and latency of requests across services and help find bottlenecks and errors, and service maps visualise dependencies. Continuous profilers like Cloud Profiler or similar tools sample stack traces from production processes with low overhead and show flame graphs over time, revealing which functions consume CPU or allocate memory, and how a release changed that. Together they answer different questions: tracing explains where in the distributed path time goes, profiling explains why a service itself is slow. For portability I prefer OpenTelemetry for instrumentation with the cloud service as a backend, and I make sure sampling and retention settings meet both debugging needs and cost constraints.
f: What does continuous profiling show?
How do traces and profiles complement each other?

q: How do you run an incident bridge: roles, communication and decision-making?
p: Assign an incident commander, scribe, communications lead and technical leads; keep a single channel, regular updates and time-boxed hypotheses.
tip: The commander coordinates, not debugs.
a: A clear structure prevents chaos. The incident commander owns coordination and decisions, delegating investigation instead of diving into it. A technical lead or leads drive diagnosis and mitigation in their areas, a scribe records the timeline, actions and decisions, and a communications lead updates stakeholders and customers on a regular cadence. Everyone works in one channel or call so information is shared, and side conversations are summarised back. The commander asks for current status, hypotheses and next steps, time-boxes them, and prefers reversible mitigation, like rollback or failover, over finding the root cause during the outage. Severity is declared early and revisited, and people are rotated to avoid fatigue in long incidents. When service is restored, the commander declares the incident mitigated, assigns follow-ups, and schedules a blameless postmortem. Practising with game days makes roles familiar before a real emergency.
f: Why should the commander not debug?
Why prefer mitigation over root cause during an outage?

q: How do you quickly determine the blast radius and customer impact of an incident?
p: Segment errors by region, tenant, version and endpoint, check SLO burn, support tickets and synthetic checks to scope who is affected.
tip: Slice by every dimension you have.
a: First I look at the symptom metrics sliced by available dimensions: region, availability zone, cluster, service version, endpoint, customer tier and tenant. If errors are concentrated in one zone or one new version, that both limits the blast radius and suggests the cause and mitigation. I compare the proportion of affected requests to the total, translating it into the number or share of users, and check how quickly the error budget is burning. External signals complement internal ones: support ticket volume, social media mentions, synthetic probes and real user monitoring. For multi-tenant systems, I identify whether specific tenants or a shared component is the problem. This scoping drives severity, communication content and who needs to be involved. I update the scope as I learn more, and record it in the timeline, because stakeholders need an honest, evolving estimate of impact.
f: Why slice by version and zone?
Which external signals help?

q: What makes a postmortem action item effective, and how do you track them?
p: Specific, owned, time-bound, prioritised by risk reduction, and tracked in the normal backlog with follow-up reviews.
cmds: # action: add alert on queue age > 5m; owner: team-a; due: 2026-11-15; priority: P1
tip: Prefer systemic fixes over reminders.
a: Weak action items say things like be more careful or improve monitoring. Effective ones are concrete, for example add an alert when queue age exceeds five minutes, with an owner, a due date and a link to the ticket. I prioritise by how much risk each removes, and favour systemic fixes such as automation, guardrails, safer defaults or removal of single points of failure over relying on humans to remember. Items are classified: detect faster, mitigate faster, prevent recurrence. They go into the same backlog and planning process as feature work, with agreed capacity, otherwise they get ignored. I review open actions regularly, report completion rates to leadership, and revisit if an action is blocked or no longer worthwhile, recording the decision. Checking whether similar incidents recur and whether detection and recovery times improved shows whether the actions worked.
f: What makes a weak action item?
How do you ensure they get done?

q: How do you handle alert storms during a major outage?
p: Silence or group symptoms, focus on the root-cause signal, designate who triages alerts, and fix the alert design afterwards.
tip: Silences need an owner and expiry.
a: In a large outage hundreds of alerts can fire, burying the signal and exhausting responders. During the incident, the commander designates one person to triage alerts, group them by common cause, and identify the root-cause alert, such as a node pool failure or a database outage. Silencing derivative alerts for a bounded duration, with a comment and an owner, keeps pagers quiet so people can think, while the main alert and the incident channel carry the information. Inhibition rules configured in advance should do much of this automatically. I make sure silences expire and are reviewed after the incident, because a forgotten silence can hide a real problem. Afterwards, I analyse which alerts were useful, add grouping and inhibition, remove redundant ones, and improve dashboards that show dependency relationships. Alert storm handling is part of on-call training and game days.
f: What should be silenced?
Why must silences expire?

q: How do you measure on-call health and reduce burnout?
p: Track pages per shift, out-of-hours pages, time to acknowledge and actionable ratio; fix noisy alerts, share load fairly and give recovery time.
cmds: # metrics: pages/shift, night pages, % actionable, MTTA, MTTR
tip: Sustainable on-call is a reliability requirement.
a: On-call is part of the system and its health affects reliability. I track pages per shift, how many occur outside working hours, the proportion that were actionable, time to acknowledge and time to resolve, and escalations. Targets such as fewer than two incidents per shift are common guidance. When numbers are bad, I address causes: eliminate or tune noisy alerts, automate frequent manual remediation, improve runbooks, and fix recurring root causes with reliability work scheduled in planning. Process measures include enough people in the rotation, fair distribution including for holidays, follow-the-sun coverage where possible, secondary responders for support, handoff notes, and compensatory time off after bad nights. I also run regular on-call reviews where engineers describe pain points, and ensure new members shadow before taking the pager. Leadership should treat unsustainable on-call as a priority issue, because exhausted responders make more mistakes.
f: Which metrics show on-call is unhealthy?
What reduces recurring pages?

q: How do you write an incident timeline and perform root cause analysis without blaming people?
p: Reconstruct events from logs and chat, ask how the system allowed the failure using techniques like five whys, and focus on contributing factors.
cmds: # timeline: 10:02 deploy; 10:07 errors rise; 10:11 page; 10:25 rollback; 10:31 recovery
tip: Why did it make sense at the time?
a: I build the timeline from objective sources: monitoring data, deployment records, audit logs and the chat transcript, noting when events happened, when they were detected and when actions were taken. Then I analyse contributing factors rather than a single root cause, because complex failures usually involve several conditions: a latent bug, a missing safeguard, a misleading alert, a gap in documentation. Techniques like the five whys help, but I keep asking how the system allowed it, not who made the mistake. A blameless approach assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew, so I ask what information they had and why the action seemed sensible. This encourages honest reporting and surfaces real weaknesses. The output includes impact, timeline, detection and response assessment, contributing factors and action items, shared widely so other teams learn. Blame hides facts, while curiosity reveals them.
f: Why avoid a single root cause?
What does blameless mean in practice?
